title: Independent Learning
description: Learning how to learn: asking good questions, finding and checking information, taking notes, planning goals, using libraries and free resources, thinking critically and, for older learners, statistics and research writing.

nodes.title: Good questions
nodes.description: Use who, what, where, when, why and how to ask clear questions.

nodes.title: Finding information
nodes.description: Use books, libraries, people and free digital resources to find answers.

nodes.title: Taking notes
nodes.description: Write down key words and ideas in your own words, with where they came from.

nodes.title: Fact or opinion
nodes.description: Tell facts from opinions and claims from evidence.

nodes.title: Checking sources
nodes.description: Judge who made a source, why, when and how they know.

nodes.title: Research plan
nodes.description: Turn a topic into a focused question and a plan to answer it.

nodes.title: Reading data
nodes.description: Averages, spread, samples, bias and correlation versus causation.

nodes.title: Writing it up
nodes.description: Write a short research paper with sources, findings and limits.

nodes.title: Curiosity
nodes.description: Enjoy not knowing yet and wanting to find out.

nodes.title: Practice
nodes.description: Mistakes help us learn; little and often works best.

nodes.title: Remembering
nodes.description: Test yourself and space practice out over days.

nodes.title: Planning
nodes.description: Set a goal, break it into steps and check progress.

nodes.title: Reflection
nodes.description: Ask what worked, what did not and what to try next.

competencies.title: Can find a book or free resource on a topic
Can tell facts from opinions and spot weak reasons
Can plan and reach a learning goal
Can use basic statistics to describe data
Can write a short research paper

items.subject: asking questions
items.title: Wonder walk
items.summary: Look around. What do you wonder about?
steps: Walk around your home or outside with an adult.
Stop and look at one thing. A snail? A cloud?
Say: "I wonder why..."
The adult writes your question down.
Pick one question to find out about together later.

check.question: Is it good to ask "why?"
check.explain: Yes! Questions help us learn new things.

check.question: You do not know an answer. What can you do?
check.explain: Not knowing yet is the start of learning.

items.adultNote: Value the question, not the answer. "Let us find out together" is a perfect response. Stay with the child outdoors.

items.subject: research skills
items.title: Picture book detective
items.summary: Find answers by looking at the pictures in a book.
steps: Choose a picture book about animals or places.
Adult asks: "Where does the bear sleep?"
Look at the pictures to find the answer.
Point to it and say what you see.
Now you ask the adult a question!

check.question: Where can we find answers?
check.explain: Books are full of answers. So are people!

check.question: Pictures can help us...
check.explain: Looking closely at pictures is real detective work.

items.adultNote: A free library card is ideal. Many public libraries also lend digital picture books.

items.subject: asking questions
items.title: Six question words
items.summary: Who, what, where, when, why and how help you ask great questions.
steps: Learn the six words: who, what, where, when, why, how.
Pick a topic you like, such as volcanoes or horses.
Write one question for each word.
Circle the question you most want answered.
Find the answer in a book or ask someone who knows.

check.question: Which word asks about a place?
check.explain: "Where" asks about a place.

check.question: Which question needs the longest answer?
check.explain: Why and how questions open up big explanations.

items.subject: libraries and free resources
items.title: Library quest
items.summary: Visit a library (in person or online) and find two books on a topic you choose.
steps: Choose a topic.
At a library, ask a librarian or use the catalogue to search your topic.
Fact books are often grouped by subject number; story books by author name.
Find two books and check the contents page and index.
Borrow them, or note the titles to look for next time.
If there is no library nearby, try a free legal digital library with an adult.

check.question: Where can you find which page talks about "teeth" in a fact book?
check.explain: The index at the back lists topics and page numbers.

check.question: Who can help you find books at a library?
check.explain: Helping people find information is a librarian's job.

items.adultNote: Library membership is usually free. Mobile or community libraries and free legal digital libraries also work. Go with the child.

items.subject: note taking
items.title: Take notes in your own words
items.summary: Notes are short key words, not copied sentences. They help you remember and explain.
steps: Read one page of a fact book or article.
Close it. Write 5 key words you remember.
Open it again and add anything important you missed.
Turn your key words into 3 short sentences in your own words.
Write the title and author of the source at the top.
Tomorrow, use only your notes to explain the topic to someone.

check.question: Good notes are mostly...
options: key words in your own words
check.explain: Short notes in your own words show you understood.

check.question: Why write down the source?
options: So you can find it again and give credit
check.explain: Researchers always record where information came from.

items.subject: critical thinking
items.title: Fact or opinion?
items.summary: A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels.
steps: Read these: "Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level." "Pizza is the best food." "Dogs have four legs." "Maths is boring."
Sort them into facts and opinions.
For each fact, say how you could check it.
Find one advert and spot the facts and the opinions in it.
Discuss: can an opinion have good reasons behind it?

check.question: "Pizza is the best food" is...
check.explain: People disagree about it, and it cannot be proven.

check.question: "Dogs have four legs" is...
check.explain: You can check it by observation.

check.question: A fact is something that can be...
check.explain: Facts can be tested or checked with evidence.

items.subject: learning how to learn
items.title: How your brain learns best
items.summary: Testing yourself and spacing practice beats re-reading. Mistakes are part of learning.
steps: Learn three tricks: test yourself (recall), space it out (little and often), mix topics.
Pick 10 facts or words you want to learn.
Day 1: learn them, then cover and test yourself.
Day 2, day 4 and day 7: test yourself again before looking.
Keep a tally of how many you remember each time.
Reflect: which trick helped most?

check.question: Which works better for remembering?
check.explain: Pulling information from memory makes it stronger.

check.question: Making a mistake while practising means...
check.explain: Mistakes show what to practise next.

items.subject: evaluating evidence
items.title: Can I trust this source?
items.summary: Use five questions to judge any article, video or post before you believe or share it.
steps: Pick one article or post about a science or news topic.
Who made it? Are they an expert or organisation you can check?
Why was it made: to inform, sell, persuade or entertain?
When was it made? Is it still up to date?
How do they know? Do they link to evidence or data?
Can you find the same claim from two other independent, reputable sources?
Give it a trust score from 1 to 5 and explain why.

check.question: A post says a drink cures illness and links to a shop. The main warning sign is...
options: It is trying to sell something
check.explain: A seller has a reason to exaggerate. Look for independent evidence.

check.question: Checking whether other reliable sources agree is called...
check.explain: Opening other sources to check a claim is a key fact-checking skill.

check.question: An old article on a fast-changing topic may be...
check.explain: Check the date, especially for science, health and technology.

items.subject: research skills
items.title: From topic to research question
items.summary: Turn a big topic into a question you can actually answer, then make a plan.
steps: Write a broad topic, e.g. "plastic".
Narrow it: where, who, when? e.g. "plastic waste in my street".
Turn it into a question: "How much plastic does my household throw away in one week?"
Check: can you answer it with the time and tools you have?
Plan: what data or sources you need, how you will collect them, and a deadline for each step.

check.question: Which is the better research question?
options: How much water does my family use on a weekday?
check.explain: It is focused, measurable and doable.

check.question: A good plan includes...
check.explain: Steps and deadlines turn a question into action.

items.subject: planning goals
items.title: Plan a 4-week learning goal
items.summary: Choose something you want to learn and build a plan you can track.
steps: Choose a goal: specific, measurable and realistic, e.g. "Learn 100 words in a new language in 4 weeks".
Break it into weekly targets.
Decide when you will practise: which days and for how long.
Make a simple tracker on paper.
At the end of each week, reflect: on track? What to change?
Celebrate effort as well as the result.

check.question: Which goal is easier to track?
options: Run 2 km without stopping by June
check.explain: A measurable goal with a date lets you see progress.

check.question: You missed a week. Best response?
check.explain: Plans are tools. Changing them is part of good planning.

items.subject: statistics
items.title: Averages and spread
items.summary: Describe data with mean, median, mode and range, and know when each one misleads.
steps: Collect 10 numbers, e.g. minutes of daily screen time across a week and a half.
Mean: add them all and divide by how many.
Median: put them in order and find the middle.
Mode: the most common value. Range: biggest minus smallest.
Add one extreme value (an outlier). Which measure changes most?
Write one sentence choosing the best average for your data and why.

check.question: Data: 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. The median is...
check.explain: In order, the middle value is 3.

check.question: For the same data the mean is...
check.explain: 30 / 5 = 6. The outlier 18 pulls the mean up.

check.question: With an extreme outlier, which average is usually more representative?
check.explain: The median is not dragged by one extreme value.

items.subject: statistics
items.title: Correlation is not causation
items.summary: Two things rising together does not prove one causes the other. Learn to look for hidden factors and bias.
steps: Example: ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
Find the confounder: hot, sunny weather drives both.
Learn about samples: who was asked, how many, and how they were chosen.
Learn about bias: survivorship, selection and self-report bias.
Find a headline claiming "X causes Y" and judge what kind of study would be needed to show cause (e.g. a randomised controlled trial).

check.question: Towns with more firefighters have more fire damage. Most likely explanation?
options: Bigger towns have more of both
check.explain: Town size is a confounder that drives both numbers.

check.question: A survey only asks people at a gym how often they exercise. This is...
check.explain: The sample is not representative of everyone.

check.question: Which design best tests cause and effect?
check.explain: Random assignment balances hidden factors between groups.

items.subject: research skills
items.title: Write a short research paper
items.summary: Investigate a focused question, collect evidence, and write a 1,000 to 1,500 word paper with sources.
steps: Choose a focused, answerable question (see "From topic to research question").
Find at least four sources, including one primary source or data set, and check each one.
Take notes with the source written next to every point.
Outline: introduction and question, method, findings, discussion, limitations, conclusion, references.
Write a first draft, then revise for clarity and evidence.
Ask someone to read it and give one strength and one improvement.
Present your findings in five minutes to your family or group.

safety.notes: Take screen breaks. If you survey people, ask permission, keep answers anonymous and never collect personal details you do not need. Do any interviews with a trusted adult aware.

materials: Your own observations or a simple survey
basic.description: Hand-write the paper using library sources and data you collect yourself.

better.description: Type the paper and make one chart from your data.

advanced.description: Use peer-reviewed or official data, cite in a consistent style and include a limitations section.

substitutions.use: Library books, newspaper archives, official printed reports and interviews
A hand-drawn table and bar chart on squared paper

check.question: A limitations section explains...
options: what your research could not show and why
check.explain: Honest limits make research more trustworthy.

check.question: Every claim from someone else should have...
check.explain: Citing gives credit and lets readers check.
